report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Simulated Survival: A Theoretical Framework for Using Immersive Virtual Reality Challenge to Target Ideation-to-Action Mechanisms of Suicide Risk

text.text: Ideation-to-action theories explain how suicidal desire develops and how some people come to act on it, but they give little guidance on interventions for the physiological state that accompanies suicidal crises.
This article proposes Simulated Survival, a theoretical framework for using controlled, demanding experiences in immersive virtual reality (VR) as an adjunct to suicide-specific care.

Drawing on the Three-Step Theory, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model, and the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide, together with research on autonomic regulation, interoception, attention under pressure, challenge appraisal, adventure-based interventions, and VR, the framework specifies three hypothesized mechanisms: interruption of suicide-specific rumination through attention captured by demanding, embodied tasks; repeated stress-recovery cycles that train autonomic and interoceptive regulation; and the pairing of high arousal with successful protective action, intended to strengthen self-preservation rather than tolerance of death-related fear.
Expectation violation is proposed as the learning process that turns short-term effects into lasting change.

Because repeated exposure to danger could raise fearlessness about death, the framework sets design rules (no suicide-method cues, no virtual death states, graded difficulty) and treats fearlessness about death as a primary safety outcome.
Eight testable propositions and a staged research path are set out.

Simulated Survival offers a testable basis for body-based digital interventions in suicide prevention, and its value depends on experimental work that tests each mechanism against active VR control conditions before any clinical trial.

An estimated 727,000 people died by suicide in 2021, and most of these deaths occurred in low-and middle-income countries (World Health Organization [WHO], 2025).
text.formatted: An estimated 727,000 people died by suicide in 2021, and most of these deaths occurred in low-and middle-income countries <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization [WHO], 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fifty years of research on risk factors has produced weak prediction, with most factors performing only slightly better than chance (Franklin et al., 2017), and machine-learning approaches have not yet solved this problem (Burke et al., 2019; Nordin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Fifty years of research on risk factors has produced weak prediction, with most factors performing only slightly better than chance <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Franklin et al., 2017)</ref>, and machine-learning approaches have not yet solved this problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Burke et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Nordin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: One response has been to study the processes that move a person toward suicidal behavior, rather than to add more distal risk markers.
The ideation-to-action framework is the clearest product of that shift.

It holds that the development of suicidal ideation and the progression from ideation to suicide attempts are separate processes with partly different causes (Klonsky & May, 2014; Klonsky et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It holds that the development of suicidal ideation and the progression from ideation to suicide attempts are separate processes with partly different causes <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Klonsky & May, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Klonsky et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Three theories lead the framework: the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide (IPTS; Joiner, 2005; Van Orden et al., 2010), the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model (IMV; O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018), and the Three-Step Theory (3ST; Klonsky & May, 2015; Klonsky et al., 2021).

text.text: Consistent with this distinction, depression, hopelessness, and most psychiatric diagnoses are associated with ideation but separate people who attempt suicide from those who only think about it poorly (May & Klonsky, 2016).
text.formatted: Consistent with this distinction, depression, hopelessness, and most psychiatric diagnoses are associated with ideation but separate people who attempt suicide from those who only think about it poorly <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(May & Klonsky, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These theories have improved the understanding of risk, but they say less about how to change the state a person is in during a suicidal crisis.
That state has a bodily side.

A metaanalysis of 22 studies found reduced heart rate variability (HRV) in adults with suicidal thoughts and behaviors, although the pooled effect was small and the association with electrodermal activity was not significant (Chowdhury et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A metaanalysis of 22 studies found reduced heart rate variability (HRV) in adults with suicidal thoughts and behaviors, although the pooled effect was small and the association with electrodermal activity was not significant <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Chowdhury et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Interoceptive deficits distinguish suicide groups in a military sample (Smith et al., 2020), and autonomic measures have been proposed as point-of-care aids to risk assessment (McCall et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Interoceptive deficits distinguish suicide groups in a military sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Smith et al., 2020)</ref>, and autonomic measures have been proposed as point-of-care aids to risk assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(McCall et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: People with suicidal thoughts and behaviors also show difficulties in decision-making and cognitive control (Gifuni et al., 2021) and an attentional bias toward suicide-related information (Richard-Devantoy et al., 2016).
text.formatted: People with suicidal thoughts and behaviors also show difficulties in decision-making and cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gifuni et al., 2021)</ref> and an attentional bias toward suicide-related information <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Richard-Devantoy et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Interventions that rely mainly on verbal reasoning may therefore be hardest to use when risk is highest.
Body-based strategies already exist.
Dialectical behavior therapy teaches crisis-survival skills that change physiology directly, including cold-water immersion of the face, brief intense exercise, and paced breathing (Linehan, 2015).
text.formatted: Dialectical behavior therapy teaches crisis-survival skills that change physiology directly, including cold-water immersion of the face, brief intense exercise, and paced breathing <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Linehan, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Heart rate variability biofeedback trains slow breathing at a resonance frequency (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014), and a meta-analysis found that it reduces self-reported stress and anxiety (Goessl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Heart rate variability biofeedback trains slow breathing at a resonance frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014)</ref>, and a meta-analysis found that it reduces self-reported stress and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Goessl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: An integrative review of mindbody interventions concluded that those working bottom-up, through body movement and emotional expression, remain under-studied compared with meditation-based approaches (Lazzarelli et al., 2024).
text.formatted: An integrative review of mindbody interventions concluded that those working bottom-up, through body movement and emotional expression, remain under-studied compared with meditation-based approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lazzarelli et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The gap, then, is not an absence of body-based tools.
It is the absence of a framework that ties such tools to the constructs of ideation-to-action theory and states which suicide-related processes they should change, by what route, and with what risks.
This article proposes such a framework, which we call Simulated Survival.

Its central claim is that demanding but controllable challenge, followed by guided physiological recovery and delivered in immersive virtual reality (VR), may act on several mechanisms named by ideation-to-action theories.
We do not claim that this intervention works.
We set out what it would have to do, how each step could be tested, and what could go wrong.
We used a narrative theoretical synthesis.
The starting point was the three ideation-toaction theories.

For each construct those theories treat as central (psychological pain, hopelessness, defeat, entrapment, connectedness, and capability), we looked for evidence on its bodily, attentional, and neural correlates and for interventions that could plausibly change it.

We then drew on research on autonomic regulation, interoception, optimal performance states, challenge and threat appraisal, adventure and nature-based interventions, and VR in mental health care and in suicide research.
This is a conceptual paper, not a systematic review.

Evidence was selected for its relevance to each proposed link, with priority given to meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and primary studies that tested a link directly, so the studies cited illustrate each link rather than exhaust it.

The framework was written to meet three requirements: each mechanism had to map onto a named theoretical construct, each had to yield a prediction that could fail, and each had to state its main risk.
No new data were collected for this article.

A generative AI tool (Claude, Opus 5.5 version; Anthropic, 2026) was used to assist with language editing and with checking reference details against bibliographic records; the authors reviewed all output and take full responsibility for the content.

The 3ST proposes that suicidal ideation begins when psychological pain is combined with hopelessness about that pain improving (Klonsky & May, 2015). Shneidman (1993) called this unbearable pain psychache.
text.formatted: The 3ST proposes that suicidal ideation begins when psychological pain is combined with hopelessness about that pain improving <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Klonsky & May, 2015)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Shneidman (1993)</ref> called this unbearable pain psychache.

text.text: Predictive processing accounts of depression suggest why hopelessness can persist despite contrary experience: negative expectations about the self and the future are held with high confidence, and information that contradicts them tends to be discounted rather than used to revise them (Kube et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Predictive processing accounts of depression suggest why hopelessness can persist despite contrary experience: negative expectations about the self and the future are held with high confidence, and information that contradicts them tends to be discounted rather than used to revise them <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kube et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: If this account applies to suicidal hopelessness, an intervention would need to produce experiences that clearly violate these expectations and are hard to dismiss.

In the IMV model, ideation emerges when defeat or humiliation is followed by entrapment, the sense that escape from one's circumstances, or from one's own thoughts and feelings, is impossible (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: In the IMV model, ideation emerges when defeat or humiliation is followed by entrapment, the sense that escape from one's circumstances, or from one's own thoughts and feelings, is impossible (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).

text.text: Gilbert and Allan (1998) described entrapment as arrested flight, a blocked urge to escape.
In a large online sample, defeat and entrapment both predicted suicide risk, and in cross-lagged analysis defeat predicted later entrapment but not the reverse (Comtois et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In a large online sample, defeat and entrapment both predicted suicide risk, and in cross-lagged analysis defeat predicted later entrapment but not the reverse <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Comtois et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Internal and external entrapment are both associated with ideation and suicidal behavior in clinical samples (Aliño-Dies et al., 2026; Rasmussen et al., 2023), and internal entrapment mediates the association between posttraumatic stress and suicidal planning (Oakey-Frost et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Internal and external entrapment are both associated with ideation and suicidal behavior in clinical samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aliño-Dies et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rasmussen et al., 2023)</ref>, and internal entrapment mediates the association between posttraumatic stress and suicidal planning <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Oakey-Frost et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Suicide-specific rumination, repeated thinking about one's suicidal thoughts and plans, has been linked to the persistence of ideation over time (Hensel & Teismann, 2026).
text.formatted: Suicide-specific rumination, repeated thinking about one's suicidal thoughts and plans, has been linked to the persistence of ideation over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Hensel & Teismann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroimaging findings fit this picture but need careful reading.

Reviews describe altered function in the default mode network (DMN), the salience network, and frontoparietal control networks in people with suicidal thoughts and behaviors (Dobbertin et al., 2023), and restingstate data link active ideation to DMN dysfunction in young people (Chin Fatt et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Reviews describe altered function in the default mode network (DMN), the salience network, and frontoparietal control networks in people with suicidal thoughts and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dobbertin et al., 2023)</ref>, and restingstate data link active ideation to DMN dysfunction in young people <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chin Fatt et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The DMN supports self-referential thought and has been associated with depressive rumination (Hamilton et al., 2015; Menon, 2023).
text.formatted: The DMN supports self-referential thought and has been associated with depressive rumination <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hamilton et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Menon, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are correlational, often come from small samples, and do not show that changing DMN activity changes ideation.
We treat them as a source of hypotheses, not as an established mechanism.
In the 3ST, connectedness to people, roles, or a sense of purpose is the main factor that keeps ideation from becoming strong when pain is high (Klonsky & May, 2015).
text.formatted: In the 3ST, connectedness to people, roles, or a sense of purpose is the main factor that keeps ideation from becoming strong when pain is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Klonsky & May, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The IPTS places thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness at the center of suicidal desire (Van Orden et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The IPTS places thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness at the center of suicidal desire <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic support is stronger for perceived burdensomeness and for the interaction of the two constructs than for thwarted belongingness alone (Chu et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic support is stronger for perceived burdensomeness and for the interaction of the two constructs than for thwarted belongingness alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Chu et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: An intervention that ignores these interpersonal needs can address only part of the motivational phase.
The step from ideation to attempt requires capability.
The IPTS describes acquired capability as reduced fear of death together with raised pain tolerance, built up through repeated painful and provocative events (Van Orden et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The IPTS describes acquired capability as reduced fear of death together with raised pain tolerance, built up through repeated painful and provocative events <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The 3ST widens the construct to dispositional, acquired, and practical capability, the last including knowledge of and access to lethal means (Klonsky & May, 2015).
text.formatted: The 3ST widens the construct to dispositional, acquired, and practical capability, the last including knowledge of and access to lethal means <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Klonsky & May, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The IMV model adds other volitional factors, among them fearlessness about death, impulsivity, access to means, and mental imagery about death (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: The IMV model adds other volitional factors, among them fearlessness about death, impulsivity, access to means, and mental imagery about death <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Imagery matters here because vivid, future-oriented images of suicide are common among depressed people with suicidal ideation (Holmes et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Imagery matters here because vivid, future-oriented images of suicide are common among depressed people with suicidal ideation <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Holmes et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Capability is usually measured as fearlessness about death (Ribeiro et al., 2014), although its factor structure is still debated (Thomas et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Capability is usually measured as fearlessness about death <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ribeiro et al., 2014)</ref>, although its factor structure is still debated <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Thomas et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fluid vulnerability theory separates a person's baseline, chronic risk from acute suicidal episodes, which are time-limited and involve linked changes in cognition, emotion, physiology, and behavior (Rudd, 2006).
text.formatted: Fluid vulnerability theory separates a person's baseline, chronic risk from acute suicidal episodes, which are time-limited and involve linked changes in cognition, emotion, physiology, and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rudd, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Simulated Survival is aimed at processes that are active in and around these episodes: suicide-specific rumination, internal entrapment, and poorly regulated arousal.
It is not designed to treat chronic vulnerability on its own.
Two bodies of work suggest that challenge-based experience can help.
The first concerns adventure and nature.

A review of 61 reviews classified wilderness and adventure therapy as one of 13 types of nature-based intervention and identified social contact and physical activity among the factors that moderate their effects (Kaleta et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A review of 61 reviews classified wilderness and adventure therapy as one of 13 types of nature-based intervention and identified social contact and physical activity among the factors that moderate their effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kaleta et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In a meta-analysis of group programs for adolescents, quasi-experimental studies showed a large pooled effect on mental health, and multi-day programs led by clinically trained or specialist facilitators tended to do better (Campbell et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis of group programs for adolescents, quasi-experimental studies showed a large pooled effect on mental health, and multi-day programs led by clinically trained or specialist facilitators tended to do better <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Campbell et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In an early intervention service for psychosis, most participants in a four-day adventure therapy trip reported gains in confidence and connectedness, although questionnaire measures of recovery did not improve at follow-up (Collin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In an early intervention service for psychosis, most participants in a four-day adventure therapy trip reported gains in confidence and connectedness, although questionnaire measures of recovery did not improve at follow-up <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Collin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Interview studies of extreme sport participants describe fear as something used and managed rather than simply endured (Brymer & Schweitzer, 2013), and an ecological account locates the value of adventure in the fit between person, task, and setting rather than in risk itself (Brymer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Interview studies of extreme sport participants describe fear as something used and managed rather than simply endured <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brymer & Schweitzer, 2013)</ref>, and an ecological account locates the value of adventure in the fit between person, task, and setting rather than in risk itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brymer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: None of this work was designed for suicide prevention, and real high-risk activities cannot ethically be prescribed to people at risk of suicide.
The second body of work concerns VR.
Immersive VR produces presence, the sense of being in the virtual place, so that perceptual and bodily responses resemble responses to real events (Slater & Sanchez-Vives, 2016).
text.formatted: Immersive VR produces presence, the sense of being in the virtual place, so that perceptual and bodily responses resemble responses to real events <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Slater & Sanchez-Vives, 2016</ref>).

text.text: An umbrella review reported benefits of VR and gamebased interventions for anxiety, depression, and stress, while noting that few randomized trials exist and that methods are often weak (Coelho & Abreu, 2026).
text.formatted: An umbrella review reported benefits of VR and gamebased interventions for anxiety, depression, and stress, while noting that few randomized trials exist and that methods are often weak <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Coelho & Abreu, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In a large randomized trial, automated VR therapy reduced agoraphobic avoidance and distress in patients with psychosis (Freeman et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In a large randomized trial, automated VR therapy reduced agoraphobic avoidance and distress in patients with psychosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Freeman et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Two quasi-experimental studies from one research group reported reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress after VR extreme-sports sessions in people with social anxiety disorder (Wang et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026); these results await independent replication.
text.formatted: Two quasi-experimental studies from one research group reported reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress after VR extreme-sports sessions in people with social anxiety disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wang et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Wei et al., 2026)</ref>; these results await independent replication.

text.text: In suicide research, VR has been used to create laboratory approximations of suicidal behavior (Franklin et al., 2019), to test dissociation as a facilitator of risk (Caulfield et al., 2022), and to examine who chooses to jump in a virtual suicide scenario (Buerke et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In suicide research, VR has been used to create laboratory approximations of suicidal behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Franklin et al., 2019)</ref>, to test dissociation as a facilitator of risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Caulfield et al., 2022)</ref>, and to examine who chooses to jump in a virtual suicide scenario <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Buerke et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal follow-up of participants in these paradigms did not find increases in suicidal thoughts or behaviors (Huang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Longitudinal follow-up of participants in these paradigms did not find increases in suicidal thoughts or behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Huang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The remaining gap is therefore specific.
Body-based crisis skills are taught as coping strategies but are not tied to ideation-to-action constructs.
Adventure programs act on these constructs only incidentally.
VR suicide paradigms study risk rather than reduce it.

No framework yet specifies how controlled challenge could act on suicide-specific rumination, entrapment, autonomic regulation, and capability, or how it could be made safe for people with suicidal ideation.

Simulated Survival is defined as a series of sessions in which a person faces a demanding but controllable challenge in immersive VR, succeeds through their own actions, and then completes guided physiological recovery.
Each session therefore has three phases: challenge, success, and recovery.
The framework proposes three mechanisms that act within sessions and one learning process that carries their effects beyond them (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The framework proposes three mechanisms that act within sessions and one learning process that carries their effects beyond them (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Note.
Targets are drawn from ideation-to-action theories.
Each session follows a challenge, success, and recovery sequence.
Three hypothesized mechanisms act within sessions; expectation violation, supported by a clinician-led debrief and safety planning, is proposed to consolidate change.
Design constraints apply throughout.
Fearlessness about death is monitored as a primary safety outcome.
HRV = heart rate variability; VR = virtual reality.
Demanding, embodied tasks compete for the attention that rumination needs.
Studies of climbers distinguish two optimal states: flow, an effortless absorption in the task, and clutch, a deliberate, effortful focus under pressure (Boudreau et al., 2022; Swann et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Studies of climbers distinguish two optimal states: flow, an effortless absorption in the task, and clutch, a deliberate, effortful focus under pressure <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Boudreau et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Swann et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Flow is reliably associated with better performance (Harris et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Flow is reliably associated with better performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Harris et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: When a task requires continuous perception and action, little capacity is left for repetitive self-focused thought.

We hypothesize that state rumination and the intensity of suicidal thoughts fall during and shortly after such tasks, and that this effect is larger than that of an equally engaging task with low arousal.
The proposed neural correlate is a shift away from DMN-dominant activity toward the salience and control networks that support externally directed attention (Menon, 2023).
text.formatted: The proposed neural correlate is a shift away from DMN-dominant activity toward the salience and control networks that support externally directed attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Menon, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A competing account, transient hypofrontality, holds that intense physical activity temporarily reduces prefrontal activity and, with it, effortful thought such as rumination (Dietrich, 2006).
text.formatted: A competing account, transient hypofrontality, holds that intense physical activity temporarily reduces prefrontal activity and, with it, effortful thought such as rumination <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dietrich, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The two accounts predict different patterns of executive performance during the task, so they can be compared directly.
For people in a suicidal state, clutch may be easier to reach than flow, because flow depends on a balance between skill and challenge that may not yet exist.
This is one reason the framework requires graded difficulty.
On its own, this mechanism would amount to distraction.
Distraction can reduce rumination in the moment, but short-term relief is not lasting change.
The framework therefore treats Mechanism 1 as the condition that opens a period in which the other mechanisms can work, not as the therapeutic effect itself.
The neurovisceral integration model links vagally mediated HRV to flexible, prefrontally guided regulation of emotion and attention (Thayer & Lane, 2000).
text.formatted: The neurovisceral integration model links vagally mediated HRV to flexible, prefrontally guided regulation of emotion and attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Thayer & Lane, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Reduced HRV in adults with suicidal thoughts and behaviors (Chowdhury et al., 2026) points to reduced flexibility in this system.
text.formatted: Reduced HRV in adults with suicidal thoughts and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Chowdhury et al., 2026)</ref> points to reduced flexibility in this system.

text.text: Simulated Survival proposes that repeated cycles of sympathetic activation during challenge, followed by guided parasympathetic recovery, can train that flexibility.

The recovery phase uses slow, paced breathing of the kind used in HRV biofeedback, which has a welldescribed physiological basis (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014) and evidence of benefit for stress and anxiety (Goessl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The recovery phase uses slow, paced breathing of the kind used in HRV biofeedback, which has a welldescribed physiological basis <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014)</ref> and evidence of benefit for stress and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Goessl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Real-time feedback during recovery lets the person see their heart rate fall as a result of what they are doing.
VR suits this mechanism because it can produce measurable stress responses.
In military police recruits, a VR scenario raised heart rate by about 26% above baseline, compared with about 34% for the same scenario performed in real life (Brinkmann et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In military police recruits, a VR scenario raised heart rate by about 26% above baseline, compared with about 34% for the same scenario performed in real life <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brinkmann et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: VR therefore induces real but somewhat weaker arousal, which is acceptable, and possibly preferable, for a clinical population.
Interoceptive accuracy may also relate to the sense of owning a virtual body, although this evidence is preliminary (Savickaite et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Interoceptive accuracy may also relate to the sense of owning a virtual body, although this evidence is preliminary <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Savickaite et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We hypothesize that the speed of HRV recovery after challenge improves across sessions, and that this improvement predicts later reductions in internal entrapment, because the person repeatedly experiences high arousal as something they can bring down.
This mechanism carries the most risk and must be stated with care.
Acquired capability is, by definition, reduced fear of death built through repeated exposure to pain and fear (Van Orden et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Acquired capability is, by definition, reduced fear of death built through repeated exposure to pain and fear <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: An intervention that repeatedly placed people in vivid near-death scenes could lower that fear through habituation, the very process the IPTS describes as dangerous.
Evidence from VR suicide research makes the concern concrete.
Some of these paradigms use stepping from a virtual height as the analogue of a suicidal act, and suicidal ideation predicts choosing to jump (Buerke et al., 2025; Franklin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Some of these paradigms use stepping from a virtual height as the analogue of a suicidal act, and suicidal ideation predicts choosing to jump <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Buerke et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Franklin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The IMV model also counts imagery about death as a volitional risk factor (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: The IMV model also counts imagery about death as a volitional risk factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Simulated Survival therefore does not aim to raise tolerance of death-related fear.
Its aim runs in the opposite direction.
Each challenge requires the person to take protective action, such as reaching shelter, steadying their footing, or guiding another person to safety, and to succeed.
High arousal is repeatedly paired with self-protective behavior and its success.
In social cognitive terms, these are mastery experiences, which Bandura (1977) identified as the most dependable source of self-efficacy expectations.
text.formatted: In social cognitive terms, these are mastery experiences, which <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bandura (1977)</ref> identified as the most dependable source of self-efficacy expectations.

text.text: In the biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat, the aim is to shift the appraisal of high-demand situations from threat toward challenge (Blascovich, 2008), a state associated with better performance (Hase et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In the biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat, the aim is to shift the appraisal of high-demand situations from threat toward challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blascovich, 2008)</ref>, a state associated with better performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hase et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The prediction is that self-efficacy rises while fearlessness about death does not.
If fearlessness about death rises, the mechanism has failed and the design must change.
The three mechanisms describe what happens within sessions.
Lasting change requires learning, and we propose that the main learning process is expectation violation.
A person who expects "I cannot escape" or "I cannot cope when my body feels like this" meets repeated, concrete evidence to the contrary: they act, they succeed, and their arousal comes down.

In predictive processing terms, these outcomes are prediction errors that could revise rigid negative expectations, provided they are salient and hard to discount (Kube et al., 2020). Riva et al. (2019) argued that VR is well placed to produce such errors because, like the brain, it works by simulating the expected sensory consequences of action.

(2019)</ref> argued that VR is well placed to produce such errors because, like the brain, it works by simulating the expected sensory consequences of action.

text.text: Exposure research points the same way.

In the inhibitory learning account, the gap between what a person expects and what happens drives new learning, and that learning holds better when it takes place across varied contexts (Craske et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In the inhibitory learning account, the gap between what a person expects and what happens drives new learning, and that learning holds better when it takes place across varied contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Craske et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This implies that scenarios should vary across sessions.
Transfer to daily life cannot be assumed.

Each session should end with a short debrief that links what happened in VR to the person's own warning signs and coping steps, and the paced-breathing skill should be written into the person's safety plan (Stanley & Brown, 2012).
text.formatted: Each session should end with a short debrief that links what happened in VR to the person's own warning signs and coping steps, and the paced-breathing skill should be written into the person's safety plan <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Stanley & Brown, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A solo VR task cannot meet the need to belong.
Two design features may partly address the IPTS constructs.
Scenarios can include a virtual companion whom the person helps to safety, which gives a direct experience of being useful to someone else and bears on perceived burdensomeness.
Sessions can also be delivered with a clinician present who joins the debrief.
Both features are hypotheses to be tested, not established effects.
Simulated Survival is proposed as an adjunct to suicide-specific care, not as a stand-alone treatment.

The intended population is adults with recent suicidal ideation who are not at imminent risk and who are already receiving clinical care, for example in outpatient services or after discharge from inpatient care.
It is not intended for use during an active crisis, when a person needs immediate assessment and safety management.
Sessions should take place in a supervised clinical setting, with a clinician able to stop a session at any point.
Four rules follow from the risks described above.
First, scenarios must contain no suicide-method cues: no heights or falls, no firearms, no drowning, and no fire, the last being relevant in regions where self-immolation occurs.
Second, there are no virtual death states.
If the person fails a step, the scenario pauses and offers an easier route, so that failure cannot reinforce defeat.
Third, difficulty is graded and adjusts to performance and to physiological response, keeping arousal within a preset range.
Fourth, success always depends on the person's own protective actions, never on being rescued.
As an illustration, consider a scenario set on a canyon floor during a rockfall.
The person must time their movements to cross open ground, help an injured hiker to a shelter, and reach safety.
All hazards are at ground level.
Once both reach the shelter, the scene calms, and a virtual coach leads two to three minutes of paced breathing while a display shows the person's heart rate.
The clinician then leads a brief debrief.
Scenario content, session length, and dose are open questions for development research.
Exclusion criteria should include current psychosis, severe dissociation, uncontrolled epilepsy or photosensitivity, and unmanaged cardiovascular disease.
People whose painful and provocative experiences overlap with a scenario's content, such as combat, need individual assessment and may need trauma-informed adaptation.

A systematic review of VR and augmented reality interventions in psychiatry found that 45 of 73 studies did not mention adverse effects at all, and that seven reported worsening symptoms or an increased risk of falls (Lundin et al., 2023).

text.text: Trials of Simulated Survival should therefore record cybersickness, distress, dissociation, and suicidal ideation before and after every session, and should treat fearlessness about death as a primary safety outcome with a predefined stopping rule.
Table 1 sets out eight propositions.
Each names a measure and the result that would count against the framework.
The choice of comparison condition matters.
A calm VR nature scene controls for immersion; an engaging but low-arousal VR task controls for absorption; and real physical exercise controls for arousal without simulation.
The framework predicts that the full challenge-success-recovery sequence will outperform each of these on its target mechanism.
If the low-arousal task performs as well, the claim that arousal is necessary is wrong, and the simpler explanation of engagement alone should be preferred.

The framework has clear limits.
Most of the evidence behind each mechanism comes from people who were not suicidal, such as climbers, military recruits, and people with social anxiety.
The neural account rests on correlational imaging data.
The VR extreme-sports studies most similar to the proposed intervention come from one research group and have not been replicated.
VR also produces weaker arousal than real-world challenge (Brinkmann et al., 2026), and whether that arousal is enough to drive the proposed learning is unknown.
text.formatted: VR also produces weaker arousal than real-world challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brinkmann et al., 2026)</ref>, and whether that arousal is enough to drive the proposed learning is unknown.

text.text: Finally, persistent and recurrent suicidal ideation are not yet consistently defined (Spangenberg et al., 2025), which complicates the choice of outcome measures.
text.formatted: Finally, persistent and recurrent suicidal ideation are not yet consistently defined <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Spangenberg et al., 2025)</ref>, which complicates the choice of outcome measures.

text.text: Access is a further concern.
Most suicides occur in low-and middle-income countries (WHO, 2025), where VR hardware and supervised delivery may be hard to provide.
Standalone headsets have reduced costs, but clinical supervision remains essential.
The meaning of adventure and challenge also differs across cultures, so scenario content will need local adaptation and testing.
We suggest a staged path based on the ORBIT model for developing behavioral treatments (Czajkowski et al., 2015).
text.formatted: We suggest a staged path based on the ORBIT model for developing behavioral treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Czajkowski et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The first stage would test each mechanism in laboratory studies, beginning with healthy volunteers and then with people who have recent ideation, against the control conditions described above.
The second stage would test feasibility, acceptability, and safety, with fearlessness about death as a primary outcome.
Only if both stages succeed would a randomized trial against an active VR control, with suicidal ideation and behavior as outcomes, be justified.

Simulated Survival proposes that demanding but controllable challenge, delivered safely in VR and followed by guided recovery, may interrupt suicide-specific rumination, train autonomic regulation, and strengthen self-preserving action under arousal.
It extends ideation-to-action theory toward intervention rather than replacing it.
Its most important feature may be its constraints: it excludes suicide-method cues, avoids virtual death, and treats any rise in fearlessness about death as a sign of failure.
Each proposition can be tested, and each could prove wrong.
That is the standard against which the framework should be judged.
